newsitem.title: INDIA: Rao's messy exit obscures achievements -newspapers.
newsitem.headline: Rao's messy exit obscures achievements -newspapers.

text.p: Indian newspapers criticised former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao on Friday, attacking him for prevaricating too long over a decision to resign as the Congress party's parliamentary leader.

Rao's mistake in not knowing when to go, forced Congress president Sitaram Kesri into issuing his former boss an ultimatum that he would be kicked out if he did not resign by Thursday. Rao finally did.

"Rao has been known to delay decisions, but this time he had to face a directive that was an order. Rao is also not known as a fighter and he had to give in," Yubaraj Ghimire, assistant editor of Outlook news weekly, told Reuters.

Rao led the party to its worst election defeat last May. Faced with a court summons in a case of fraud, he resigned as party president in September to make way for Kesri amid allegations of corruption surrounding Rao and his aides.

"The ignominy of the past few days may not do proper justice to the career of a man who had his share of achievements while in office, but there are many that are certain he deserved worse," the Asian Age newspaper said in an editorial.
The editorials dished out meaty criticism of Rao, who dominated Indian politics after taking over as Congress president following Rajiv Gandhi's assassination in 1991.
But they also praised Rao's courage in introducing a liberal economic reform programme to shake off the stultifying effects of decades of central planning that Congress had championed.
"Future historians are likely to assign to Mr Rao a more exalted place than what contemporary politicians and observers of politics would grant him," the Hindustan Times said.

Three separate cases involving allegations of corruption, forgery and fraud are widely seen as having damaged the image of the Congress party, which has ruled India for all but five years since independence from Britain in 1947.
The 75-year-old Rao has denied any wrong-doing in the cases, but his political credibility suffered.
"In a sense the Rao era had come to symbolise corruption at high places eroding the credibility of not only the party but the democratic polity as a whole," the Hindu said.
The Times of India supported the call for Congress to reintroduce democratic internal elections, which were reduced to rubber-stamp formalities since Indira Gandhi commandeered the party in 1969.

"A beginning should be attempted with the leadership of the parliamentary party. Let all those interested throw their hats in the ring and fight it out in the best democratic tradition of the secret ballot," the newspaper said.
